talks.title: Building & Defending a Machine Learning Malware Classifier: Taking 3rd at MLSEC
talks.teaser: Walks through building a malware classifier, then attacking rival models in an adversarial ML competition.
talks.summary:
Andy Applebaum recounts his solo entry into the 2021 Machine Learning Security Evasion Competition, where he built a static detector for Windows executables and then tried to break the models submitted by other entrants. The talk opens with the case for adversarial machine learning, explaining how small, deliberate changes can fool an otherwise accurate classifier, and why the competition imposed strict limits on runtime and false positives.

The middle section covers the build. The detector was trained on public malware and benign corpora, plus a large set of adversarial variants generated with open-source evasion tools and templated payload generation. An off-the-shelf baseline did poorly on the evasive samples, while retraining on the generated variants helped considerably. The final model combined several trained candidates and a stateful check that compared new submissions against recent ones. It finished third.

For the attack half, the speaker queried rival classifiers, trained a surrogate model to mimic them, and used reinforcement-learning evasion tools against it. Reconnaissance and other frameworks were also tried, and many submissions were filtered out or failed to evade. Traditional packing and encryption tools proved far more effective at evading classifiers that had no training on them. The closing lessons cover planning disk and compute resources, keeping careful experiment records, separating training and test data, and the ways contest scoring can be gamed.

talks.title: Worst of Cybersecurity Reporting
talks.teaser: Dissects 2021 tech news stories that got privacy policies, press releases and technical details wrong, and how to do better.
talks.summary:
Yael Grauer and David Huerta return with their annual critique of technology journalism, this year covering stories from 2021. They group the weakest coverage into four failings: not reading a company's privacy policy or terms, repeating press releases without checking them, leaving key details vague, and relying on sources without relevant expertise. Examples include a messaging app's data-sharing prompt that was not actually new, an open-source audio editor's analytics being labeled spyware, a quantum computing claim that rested on a company's announcement, and a mobile voting app story that gave vendor rebuttals equal weight without contacting the researchers involved.

The middle of the talk argues that the problem spans the whole ecosystem, not just individual writers. Deadlines, editors rewriting headlines, public relations staff who speak only off the record, and companies with unclear data practices all contribute. The speakers suggest that reporters read documentation and compare changes, contact everyone named in an allegation, verify vendor claims independently, and make sure headlines match the reporting. Researchers criticizing an article should explain their objections in detail, and companies should be transparent and willing to put named spokespeople on the record.

The question-and-answer section covered public records requests, which the speakers described as slow and frustrating, with some agencies narrowing or closing requests on technicalities. They recommended vetting anyone who asks for an interview and leaning on community resources for handling records requests. The closing message is that careful reading, cross-checking and expert sourcing matter more than speed.

talks.title: Observations from Social Engineering my way Through a Pandemic
talks.teaser: Shows how COVID-19 themed pretexts shifted phishing and vishing results during remote work, and the ethical choices behind them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how one social engineering consultant changed phishing and vishing engagements once the pandemic pushed workforces into remote work. Attackers quickly used COVID-19 as a lure, and the speaker found employees were more likely to respond to messages about the crisis, especially when new login portals, VPN changes and unfamiliar processes added confusion. Pretexts were built around the consequences of the pandemic rather than impersonating health agencies, and the speaker avoided promising bonuses that could later be revoked.

Several observations stood out. Many pre-pandemic pretexts, such as fake dress code notices and IT impersonation, still worked with little change. Some clients opted out because of budget cuts or concern about adding stress, and one point of contact clicked a test email even after being warned. Phone calls were especially effective when people were eager to talk, though that made some of the stories uncomfortable to tell. Success rates rose and fell with news about virus variants, and lures moved from health alerts to stimulus checks and student loan extensions.

The closing argument favors continued user education, preparing staff for the next crisis-themed lure, and keeping phishing emails simple, since employees often expect phishing to be full of typos. The speaker encouraged ongoing debate about the ethics of using crisis themes in testing and pointed to published research on COVID-19 phishing emails.

talks.title: What I Learned After my First Year as a Security Analyst
talks.teaser: Shares practical lessons from a first year as a SOC analyst, covering log reading, alert limits, and career survival.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a plain definition of the analyst role: take in logs and alerts, investigate them, and decide whether a threat is present, with the response often set by organizational policy rather than by the analyst. The speaker argues that networking fundamentals, clear communication, attention to detail, and a curious, hacker-style mindset matter more than any particular degree or certification.

The middle section covers practical lessons. Reading raw log data at the source helps when parsers miss fields or hostnames and IP addresses get swapped. Threat intelligence knowledge is essential for quickly learning about events such as Log4j. Mistakes are inevitable and should be handled as learning opportunities, while escalations may never be fixed or even acknowledged. Missing logs limit what an investigation can prove, and every SOC has weaknesses that depend on its alert rules and on analysts' understanding of them. The speaker also shares tips for sleeping through night shifts and warns against staying in a role that offers no growth.

The closing section offers ways to start learning. Graylog, Kibana, and trial or free editions of commercial SIEMs can run on a home lab, and Splunk's Boss of the SOC datasets give practice material. The Open SOC competition run at DEF CON simulates analyst and threat-hunting work. Incident response is presented as a natural next step from analyst work.

talks.title: Building the Cybersecurity Pipeline: A Call to Action
talks.teaser: Explains why the cybersecurity talent gap persists and surveys programs that aim to build a workforce pipeline.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the gap between the large number of unfilled cybersecurity roles and the people able to fill them. Entry-level listings often demand degrees, certifications or years of experience that newcomers lack. Job-ad analysis shows mismatched requirements, and the speaker argues that credentials alone do not make someone ready. Networking, volunteering, honest self-assessment and a realistic, time-bound goal are presented as practical steps for anyone entering the field.

The middle surveys efforts already underway. Examples include a university security operations center where students gain real work experience, an apprenticeship model, credit transfer from community colleges to universities, high school programs starting in ninth grade, and nonprofit and industry partnerships that offer stipends and free training. The speaker also argues that cyber safety belongs in everyday digital education and that employers should invest in workers and consider candidates without traditional credentials.

The closing call to action asks applicants to demonstrate their own skills and ask for help, professionals to mentor and share their paths, and organizations to donate equipment, fund teachers and open doors for younger people. The session ends with questions about program length and how curricula can keep pace with industry needs.
